note: Curated cross-branch confusable pairs. These are perceptually legitimate confusions that the tree structure under-credits, because the two attributes sit in different branches (or different categories) despite tasting alike. Weight is a fraction of a perfect score; the engine awards max(structural base, weight * 100). Pairs are symmetric. Ring-3 siblings are deliberately absent - the sibling tier already credits those, and an entry that scores below its own structural base is dead weight (enforced by test).
reviewTarget: Q1 KR3.2 - inter-rater agreement >= 0.7 across 3 Q-graders. Until then these weights are one practitioner's judgement, not consensus.

pairs.note: Category-level. Both are Maillard products of the same roast, and telling them apart is one of the hardest calls a beginner faces. The wheel's ring order places Spices between them, so the geometry scores them as unrelated - they are anything but.
Category-level. Sugar browning produces both: caramelisation and roast character are two points on one continuum with no sharp edge. The wheel separates them by three positions.
Category-level. Toasted kernel and cooked sugar share Maillard aromatics and routinely co-occur; tasters split on which one leads.

Malic acid is the dominant acid in apples - the sensation and the fruit reference are the same thing seen from two directions. Beginners taste 'green apple' and reach for the fruit; graders name the acid.
Softer, rounder malic expression reads as pear rather than apple.
Same acid/fruit duality as malic-apple. The distinction worth teaching: citric acid is the sensation, lemon carries aromatics on top of it.
Lime reads as citric acid with a greener, more pungent aromatic.
Lower-intensity citric with sweetness present pulls the call toward orange.
The fruity/fermented boundary. Winey is grape aromatics plus alcohol and acetic lift; drop the lift and tasters say grape.
Overripe strawberry sits exactly on the line between desirable fruit and incipient ferment. A classic split-the-table call.
Naturals pushed hard in drying give blueberry-like intensity that is really early ferment. Beginners hear 'blueberry natural' as praise; it is often a process fault.
Acetic lift is the leading edge of ferment character - same defect pathway, different intensity.
Butyric (rancid butter, vomit-like) is a ferment marker; naming the specific acid is the harder, more useful call.
Isovaleric (sweaty, cheesy) likewise indicates over-fermentation.
Rancid-dairy and animal notes overlap heavily at low intensity.
Sweaty/cheesy character is routinely called animalic by untrained panels.
Dried fruit and brown sugar converge in darker roasts - both are concentrated sugar with cooked-fruit aromatics.
Prune and molasses are the same dark, syrupy register; roast level usually decides which word a taster reaches for.
Both sit in a sweet, fatty, mildly lactonic space. Crossing a category boundary here is a small error, not a large one.
The nutty/cereal boundary. Toasted almond and toasted grain share the same Maillard aromatics.
Malt adds sweetness to the same toasted-nut register.
Peanut and raw grain overlap strongly in under-developed roasts.
The hardest call in staling. Cereal is a roast character; papery is age. Same dry, dusty impression, opposite diagnosis.
As above - cardboard is oxidised lipid, not roast, but the two read alike to a new palate.
Stale coffee flattens toward a dry cereal impression.
Cured leaf versus sweetened aromatic blend. The tree only knows they share a category, so it scores them as far apart as Blackberry and Raisin; perceptually they are near-neighbours.
Dry, aged, woody character underlies both; pipe tobacco adds sweetness.
Old-crop woodiness is frequently called tobacco.
Dark chocolate is largely a roast artefact. Where roast ends and cocoa begins is a genuine judgement call, not an error.
Heavy roast pushes cocoa toward smoke; the two coexist more often than they separate.
Sugar browning is a continuum. Caramelized and brown-roast are two points on it, and the boundary is a matter of degree.
Smoke and phenol share the same aromatic family, but one is roast and the other is a serious defect. Worth partial credit and a firm correction.
Near-synonymous in practice. Phenolic is the diagnostic term; medicinal is what tasters say first.
Eugenol drives both. Clove is the pleasant expression of the same compound family that reads as medicinal when it dominates.
As above - the clove/phenol axis is a real perceptual continuum, not a mistake.

Natural vanilla is complex and floral; vanillin is the single synthetic note. They branch directly off the category, so the tree gives them no more credit than an unrelated pair - perceptually they are almost adjacent.
Sweet aromatics is the umbrella impression; vanilla is one of its most common components.
Honey is often what tasters mean by a general sweetness impression.
Maple and vanilla overlap in the sweet-aromatic register.
Milk-chocolate character and molasses share sweetness plus cooked-sugar depth.
Jasmine tea exists for a reason. Black tea is tannic and floral; jasmine is the floral without the tannin.
Both are dried-flower infusions; chamomile is softer and hay-adjacent.
Chamomile sits directly on the floral/hay boundary. Crossing it is a defensible call, not a miss.
Beany terminates at ring 2 while peapod sits a level deeper, so the tree separates two attributes that are almost the same sensation.
Raw is under-development in the roast; under-ripe is under-development in the fruit. Same green impression, different cause - a distinction worth drilling.
Both terminate at ring 2 and both describe trigeminal sharpness rather than aroma; the tree scores them as distant when they are close.
Cinnamon-like warmth is often a roast artefact rather than an origin character.
